strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem: spectral data silos caused by camera-specific channel dimensions and wavelength coverage, which blocks cross-camera and cross-modality transfer.

Clean and well-motivated architecture: wavelength positional encoding (continuous Fourier features) plus a self-attention/cross-attention query module is a principled way to make representations channel-dimension invariant while capturing inter-channel dependencies, which prior channel-adaptive methods (Hyve, HyperFree, Spectral Adapter) neglect.

Novel, well-integrated spectral-spatial self-supervised pre-training (CARL-SSL) combining channel masking with I-JEPA-style feature-space prediction, with VICReg loss; operates efficiently in feature space.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct domains (medical, automotive, satellite) with consistent gains over camera-specific and channel-invariant baselines; nice qualitative demonstration of cross-modality knowledge transfer (pole class in HSICity).

Thorough ablations on positional encoding scale and number of queries, FLOP/parameter comparison showing favorable capacity-cost trade-off vs. SpectralGPT+, and detailed supplementary with pseudo-code and data-generation protocol supporting reproducibility.
Pre-training efficiency claim is supported: CARL-SSL beats SpectralGPT+ using ~1% of the pre-training data with higher spectral resolution.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty in isolation: the method is essentially a combination of known components (Fourier feature encodings, Perceiver-style latent queries, I-JEPA, VICReg); the contribution is the adaptation and integration rather than fundamentally new ideas.

Some headline comparisons are close relative to reported uncertainty: e.g., in Table 1, CARL (48.6) vs. Hyve (48.0) with overlapping 95% confidence intervals, and CARL-SSL (50.1, CI 47.2-52.4) also overlaps Hyve's interval; the +1.6 mIoU improvement over SpectralGPT+ in Table 2 is modest.

The in silico medical experiment relies on synthetically simulated multispectral cameras (Gaussian filters applied to hyperspectral data); real-world cross-camera behavior in medicine is not directly demonstrated, so the 'proof of concept' is somewhat idealized.

Pre-training scale is small (11,483 HSI patches, small 12-block model), leaving claims of scalability and 'backbone for future spectral foundation models' under-supported; no experiments with larger models or data.

Experiments are confined to semantic segmentation; other downstream tasks (classification, detection, spectral reconstruction) are not evaluated, limiting evidence of general-purpose representation quality.

The approach assumes accurate per-channel wavelength metadata is available at train and test time; the paper does not discuss sensitivity to wavelength calibration errors or cameras with poorly specified band centers, a realistic concern in practice.

Channel sub-sampling to 32 channels for memory reasons and dataset mixing choices (hand-annotated HSICity test images incorporated into training) introduce protocol details whose impact on comparability is not fully ablated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: spectral heterogeneity across cameras (varying channel counts and wavelength coverage) that fragments data into camera-specific silos and prevents unified pre-training.

The architecture is well-motivated: wavelength positional encoding (Fourier Features over continuous wavelengths) plus Perceiver-style learned query compression into a camera-agnostic embedding is a clean, sensible design for channel-dimension invariance.
Evaluation spans three distinct domains (medical, automotive, satellite) with segmentation tasks, and includes relevant channel-invariant baselines (HyperFree, Hyve, Spectral Adapter, SpectralGPT+).

Ablations on the positional encoding scale σ and number of queries K are informative (e.g., catastrophic drop without PE), and the FLOPs analysis showing a favorable cost trade-off against SpectralGPT+ is a useful addition.
The supplementary provides pseudo-code, loss decompositions, and implementation details, supporting reproducibility of the method itself.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: each component is a known technique (sinusoidal/Fourier positional encoding, Perceiver-style query cross-attention, I-JEPA + VICReg losses). The contribution is primarily a combination and adaptation of existing machinery to the spectral-camera setting; the repeated 'first approach' claims feel overstated relative to the conceptual leap.

The headline in silico proof-of-concept relies on simulated multispectral cameras (Gaussian filter models fit to a single real camera) on a small, private porcine dataset (254 images, 12 subjects). This weakens both external validity and reproducibility; no public hyperspectral medical benchmark is used.

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest in the real-world experiments: +1.5 mIoU over the non-pre-trained variant on HSICity and +1.6 mIoU over SpectralGPT+ on SegMunich. Given wide 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 50.2–53.2), it is unclear the differences are statistically meaningful, and pre-training data differ across compared methods, complicating attribution.

The camera-agnostic advantage on HSICity is driven largely by the 'pole' class label transfer from Cityscapes; the benefit is concentrated on one class rather than broad robustness, which the aggregate mIoU framing somewhat overstates.

Evaluation is restricted to semantic segmentation with a relatively small backbone (12 blocks, D=384); there is no evidence of scaling behavior, no classification/retrieval or linear-probe evaluation, and no direct test of out-of-distribution cameras unseen at training time in the real-world settings.

Several key design choices (e.g., EVA-02/DINOv2 initialization of the spectral and spatial encoders, interaction between initialization and the SSL strategy, the choice of L=4 spectral-cross-attention stages) are not ablated, so the source of the improvements is not fully disentangled.
Positioning against concurrent channel-adaptive methods could be more careful; some claims about competitors (e.g., fusion methods requiring all modalities) are asserted without empirical support.

strengths: Clear and relevant problem statement: cross-camera spectral heterogeneity is a genuine bottleneck for spectral image analysis, and the paper positions itself well against existing channel-adaptive approaches (HyperFree, Hyve, Spectral Adapter, SpectralGPT+) with a well-written related work section that clearly identifies the gap (lack of explicit inter-channel correspondence modeling).

Well-motivated and technically coherent architecture: wavelength positional encoding (continuous Fourier features) combined with learned query representations via self-/cross-attention is a sensible design that resolves the channel dimension while remaining wavelength-aware, unlike prior spatial-only adaptations.

Comprehensive multi-domain evaluation: experiments span medical (organ segmentation), automotive (urban scene segmentation with real HSI/RGB cross-modality transfer), and satellite (land cover classification) domains, addressing both simulated (RQ1) and real-world (RQ2) spectral heterogeneity.

Strong empirical results with statistical rigor: 95% confidence intervals reported, systematic heterogeneity stress tests (Fig. 5), the 'pole' class transfer experiment is a compelling qualitative demonstration of cross-modal knowledge transfer, and CARL-SSL outperforms SpectralGPT+ using ~1% of the pre-training data with roughly half the FLOPs (Table 4).

Ablations directly support the core design choices (wavelength PE with σ=3, K=8 queries), including a dramatic drop without PE (18.3 vs 61.5 mIoU), and pseudo-code in the supplementary improves reproducibility.

The CARL-SSL strategy is a non-trivial adaptation of I-JEPA to the spectral domain (channel masking with wavelength-conditioned mask tokens in feature space), which is a reasonable and novel combination for camera-agnostic pre-training.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural integration rather than fundamental: all components (Fourier feature positional encoding, learned query tokens with cross-attention, I-JEPA-style latent masking, VICReg) are well-established; the contribution is their combination for the camera-agnostic setting. This limits the conceptual depth of the contribution.

The 'first camera-agnostic framework' claim is strong; while plausible, it hinges on how one defines camera-agnostic, and comparisons to some potentially relevant cross-modality/cross-sensor approaches appear incomplete.

The medical proof-of-concept relies on a synthetic multispectral simulation (Gaussian filter functions) from a single private porcine hyperspectral dataset, which weakens the external validity of RQ1 and hurts reproducibility (private dataset, no public release mentioned).

Scale of validation is modest: the pre-training corpus for CARL-SSL is ~11k hyperspectral images, and the model is small (12 blocks, dim 384); scalability claims of the approach as a 'foundation model backbone' are not yet substantiated by large-scale experiments.

Some baseline setups are not fully comparable: the camera-specific baseline in Table 1 is pre-trained on Cityscapes and fine-tuned only on HSICity, while channel-invariant baselines are trained on both; this favors CARL's exposure to RGB annotations in the transfer experiment, and architectural backbones differ across baselines (U-Net vs ViT/Swin).

No ablation isolating the contribution of CARL-SSL components (spectral masking strategy, VICReg vs alternatives such as simple MSE on teacher targets, EMA teacher), and no analysis of failure cases or sensitivity to out-of-distribution wavelength ranges (e.g., channels outside the 418–2450 nm range used in pre-training).

Computational analysis covers FLOPs but not training/inference wall-clock times or memory, which matter for the claimed efficiency advantage, and the per-channel patch-wise spectral encoder introduces its own sequential cost for very high C.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem in spectral imaging: camera-specific data silos that prevent cross-camera knowledge transfer, a real bottleneck in medical, automotive, and remote-sensing applications.

The proposed architecture is well-motivated: wavelength positional encoding (Fourier features over actual wavelengths) combined with a self-attention/cross-attention module with K learned spectral representations cleanly achieves channel-dimension invariance while remaining wavelength-aware, and scales only linearly with the number of channels (unlike SpectralGPT+).

The CARL-SSL framework is a thoughtful combination of a novel feature-based spectral masked-prediction objective (with wavelength-conditioned mask tokens and VICReg regularization) with I-JEPA spatial pre-training, and the ablation (Tab. 3c) convincingly shows the spectral SSL term prevents spectral representation collapse (+10.5 OA).

Extensive evaluation across three distinct domains (private medical HSI, RGB+HSI urban driving, satellite) with both simulated filter-based spectral heterogeneity and real-world cross-camera data, and a broad set of competitive baselines (Spectral Adapter, HyperFree, Hyve, DOFA, SpectralGPT+, SatMAE, camera-specific models).

Good supporting analyses: ablations of positional encoding, aggregation strategy, K, and embedding dimension; FLOP/parameter comparison showing a favorable cost trade-off; feature variance decomposition (organ class explains 61.6% of variance vs. 0.6% for sensor) and t-SNE analysis supporting the camera-agnostic claim; pseudo-code and implementation details aid reproducibility; hyperparameters held constant across domains.
weaknesses: Some headline results are not statistically compelling: in Tab. 2, CARL-SSL (50.1 [47.2-52.4]) vs. DOFA (49.6 [46.8-51.6]) and CARL (48.6 [45.6-51.0]) have heavily overlapping 95% confidence intervals, and in Tab. 5 the 1.4 mIoU gain over DOFA is modest relative to interval widths. The robustness narrative (Fig. 5) is more convincing than the absolute superiority claims.

The core medical experiment relies on a private porcine organ dataset, limiting reproducibility and external validation of the most controlled 'proof-of-concept' claims; no public medical spectral benchmark is used.

Fairness concerns in some comparisons: the camera-specific baseline is trained only on the HSI subset while camera-agnostic methods are trained on the combined RGB+HSI data (Tab. 2, 3b), so part of the gain may reflect access to more labeled data rather than the representation itself; Tab. 1's four-criteria comparison is also a self-defined taxonomy that the paper wins by construction.

CARL is significantly more expensive than channel-adaptive baselines (120.5G vs. 6.4G FLOPs, ~19x over EVA-02/Hyve), and the paper leans on strong external initializations (DINOv2-initialized spectral encoder blocks, ImageNet-pretrained EVA-02), which makes it harder to attribute gains purely to the proposed camera-agnostic design.

Practical compromises that slightly undercut the camera-agnostic story: hyperspectral images are downsampled to 64 channels for pre-training and randomly subsampled to 32 channels when C > 32 during downstream training; the ideal channel count and interpolation behavior of the wavelength PE across very different spectral sampling regimes (e.g., Sentinel-2 vs. EnMAP SWIR at 2,445 nm) are not analyzed.

Scale of pre-training (78k iterations, one H200) is small relative to 'foundation model' positioning in the abstract/discussion; the claim that CARL is a 'backbone for future spectral foundation models' is speculative relative to the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practically important bottleneck in spectral imaging: camera-specific data silos with heterogeneous channel dimensionality and wavelength coverage. The motivation and positioning (Table 1) are clear and well-researched.

The proposed spectral encoder is well-motivated: wavelength positional encoding provides an elegant mechanism for establishing cross-camera channel correspondences, and the self-attention/cross-attention design with K learnable spectral representations keeps computation linear in the spectral dimension (favorable FLOP profile vs. SpectralGPT+ per Table 8).

Evaluation is unusually broad and well-designed: three domains (medical, automotive, satellite), a controlled in-silico protocol that isolates spectral variability while preserving geometry, real-world filter synthesis as a sanity check, and cross-modality transfer tests (removed 'pole'/'traffic light' classes) that directly probe the central claim of camera-agnostic knowledge transfer.

Baselines are appropriate and current (Spectral Adapter, HyperFree, Hyve, DOFA, SpectralGPT+, SatMAE), trained under a common protocol, with confidence intervals reported; the ablations (Table 6) show the wavelength PE is essential (18.3 vs. 61.5 mIoU), supporting the core design choice.

The analysis of feature representations (Table 10, t-SNE in Fig. 6) provides direct evidence that learned features encode semantics rather than sensor identity, and the SSL ablation (Table 3c) quantifies the contribution of the spectral SSL objective (+10.5 OA) and shows it prevents spectral representation collapse.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: pseudo-code for both forward and training passes, detailed hyperparameters, publicly available datasets for two of three domains, and a stated single-GPU (40GB) compute budget.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is moderate: the spectral encoder is essentially a Perceiver-style latent attention module with Fourier-feature positional encoding over wavelengths, combined with I-JEPA (spatial) and VICReg (loss). Each ingredient is well-executed but the primary novelty lies in the combination and adaptation rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

Several headline comparisons are not statistically decisive. In Table 2, CARL (48.6) does not beat DOFA (49.6); only CARL-SSL (50.1) does, and the 95% CIs overlap substantially across nearly all methods. Similarly, in Table 4 the m-cashew-plantation gain (18.9 vs. 18.7) and the SegMunich fine-tuning gain (50.9 vs. 49.5) are modest relative to interval widths, weakening the claim of consistent superiority.

The medical dataset (private porcine organ collection) is not publicly available, so the most controlled experiment (RQ1) cannot be reproduced by the community; the in-silico camera simulation, while careful, is a proof of concept rather than evidence on real cross-camera hardware variation.

Potential confound from strong initialization: the spectral encoder is initialized from DINOv2 weights and the spatial encoder from EVA-02 ImageNet SSL weights. The paper does not disentangle how much of the performance derives from the proposed architecture/SSL versus these large-scale pre-trained initializations, which several baselines may not equally benefit from.

The 'first approach' claims (contributions 1 and 2) are stated strongly; given the rapid pace of the field (HyperFree, DOFA, AnySat, Galileo, SpectralEarth all cited as 2024-2025 preprints), the novelty positioning relies on a particular taxonomy (Table 1) that may be contested, and some cited competitors are arXiv preprints whose final versions may narrow the gap.

Practical limitations are acknowledged but not fully resolved: the higher computational cost (120.5G FLOPs vs. 6.4G for channel-adaptive approaches is a ~19x overhead), spatial-resolution heterogeneity across sensors, and the channel-sampling workaround (subsampling to 32 channels) suggest scalability concerns for true hyperspectral inputs in practice.

The paper would benefit from an analysis of failure modes or cases where wavelength positional encoding breaks down (e.g., cameras with mismatched spectral ranges, calibrated vs. uncalibrated reflectance), which is highly relevant for the medical deployment scenarios emphasized in the motivation.

strengths: Addresses a real and important bottleneck in spectral imaging: camera-specific data silos that prevent joint model development across sensors. The problem formulation and positioning against existing approaches (Table 1) is clear and well-motivated.

The proposed spectral encoder is well-designed and reasonably efficient: wavelength positional encoding (Fourier features over nm-wavelengths) combined with a Perceiver-style self-attention/cross-attention readout distills an arbitrary number of channels into K learned spectral representations, making the model genuinely channel-invariant while scaling linearly in C.

The spatio-spectral self-supervision strategy (spectral channel masking with feature-space prediction via VICReg, combined with I-JEPA spatial pre-training) is a sensible and non-trivial adaptation; the ablation showing collapse of spectral representations with spatial-only SSL (Table 3c, +10.5 OA) is a convincing argument for the spectral loss term.

Broad evaluation across three heterogeneous application domains (medical, automotive, satellite) with both simulated (controlled Gaussian filters, real filter responses) and real-world cross-camera variation, which is more thorough than typical papers in this area.

Good ablation coverage (positional encoding, aggregation strategy, K, embedding dimension) and an honest computational complexity analysis (Appendix B) that reports the model's substantially higher FLOP count rather than hiding it.
Above-average reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, pseudo-code for both forward pass and SSL training step, and mostly public datasets.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is moderate. The core components are known techniques: sinusoidal Fourier features as positional encoding, learnable queries with cross-attention (Perceiver-style set encoder), and a JEPA/VICReg-style feature-prediction SSL recipe. The contribution is a competent combination and adaptation to the spectral domain rather than a fundamentally new method, which weakens the 'first approach' framing.

Evidence for superiority over the strongest baselines is not always statistically convincing. In Table 2, CARL-SSL (50.1 [47.2; 52.4]) and DOFA (49.6 [46.8; 51.6]) have overlapping 95% confidence intervals; the m-forestnet probing result (Table 4) and several Table 3 entries also show small gaps, and Table 3a reports no confidence intervals at all. The headline claim of consistent outperformance is stronger than the evidence in several places.

Potential baseline fairness concerns. CARL heavily leverages strong RGB pre-trained checkpoints (spectral encoder initialized from DINOv2, spatial encoder from EVA-02 with ImageNet MIM weights), and baselines were integrated with 'either a U-Net or a ViT-based architecture, depending on which proved most compatible.' The initialization and architecture matching between CARL and baselines is not described rigorously enough to rule out confounded comparisons.

The computational cost is a significant practical concern: CARL requires ~120.5G FLOPs versus 6.4-8.0G for Hyve/HyperFree/DOFA (roughly a 15-19x increase) and 28.9M parameters, yet some of the resulting performance gains fall within the confidence intervals of the far cheaper channel-adaptive methods. The cost-benefit trade-off is not clearly favorable.

The satellite experiment (the strongest scaling demonstration) compares only against DOFA-B and SpectralGPT+; HyperFree and Hyve are absent from Tables 4-5, and the fine-tuning gain over the strongest baseline is 1.4 mIoU, which is modest.

Internal consistency issues weaken reproducibility of the medical experiments: the organ dataset is private (only 254 images from 12 subjects), no code release is stated (pseudo-code only), and for SSL pre-training hyperspectral images are downsampled to 64 channels while inference-time training subsamples to 32 channels, so the evaluated models do not operate on the full spectra that the motivation emphasizes.

Several claims rely on the related-work table rather than direct comparisons: Table 1's checklist is favorable to the authors, but HyperFree/Hyve/DOFA lack spatio-spectral SSL partially by design scope, and the 'first' claims would benefit from more careful hedging.

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated gap: the lack of camera-agnostic, spatio-spectral representation learning for spectral imaging, where existing methods are either channel-invariant but spatial-only (DOFA, HyperFree, Hyve, SMARTIES, Copernicus-FM) or spatio-spectral but camera-specific (SpectralGPT).

Technically sound and clearly described architecture: wavelength-based positional encoding to align channels across cameras, a Perceiver-style self-attention/cross-attention spectral encoder with K learned spectral representations, and a feature-based spectral SSL objective (VICReg) combined with I-JEPA spatial pre-training. Pseudo-code (Algorithms 1, 2) and hyperparameters support reproducibility.

Comprehensive, large-scale cross-domain validation spanning medical imaging, automotive scene segmentation, and satellite imaging, with both simulated (Gaussian and real-filter-derived multispectral) and real-world cross-camera variations (e.g., HSICity vs. Cityscapes; OOD sensors like Gaofen-5, LandSat-8, RGB).

Strong and appropriate baselines, including recent foundation models (SpectralGPT+, DOFA, Copernicus-FM, SMARTIES, Galileo, Croma), with a fair-complexity comparison (Tab. 11) showing CARL's favorable compute-performance trade-off (fewest parameters among spatio-spectral options; best average rank 1.6 across 11 benchmarks).

Thorough ablation studies (positional encoding, aggregation, K, embedding dimension, spectral vs. spatial SSL components) and convincing additional analyses: variance decomposition showing sensor explains only 0.6% of feature variance, t-SNE disentanglement analysis, and channel-subsampling as cost reduction demonstrating genuine camera-agnostic behavior.

Insightful downstream evidence of cross-modality knowledge transfer, e.g., the 'pole' class learned from RGB labels and applied to hyperspectral test data, and +10.5 OA from spectral SSL mitigating representation collapse.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is primarily compositional rather than fundamental: wavelength positional encoding (Fourier features), Perceiver-style cross-attention with learned latents, I-JEPA, and VICReg are all established components; the contribution lies mainly in their combination and adaptation to the spectral domain, which may limit perceived conceptual novelty.

Statistical significance of headline results is not always established: in Tab. 2 the 95% confidence intervals for CARL-SSL [47.2; 52.4], CARL [45.6; 51.0], and DOFA [45.4; 50.0] overlap substantially, weakening the claim of 'superior performance' in the automotive setting; only the average-rank evidence across 11 datasets is more persuasive.

The in-silico proof of concept (Sec. 4.1) relies on a private porcine organ dataset, limiting reproducibility of one of the three experimental pillars, and the synthetic multispectral generation, while carefully designed, is still a simulation.

The abstract and introduction claim 'outperforming' across all experiments, but some results are closer to parity (e.g., SegMunich fine-tuning 50.9 vs. DOFA 49.5; m-eurosat below SMARTIES and DOFA); claims should be calibrated to the evidence.

Computational cost is acknowledged but the practical overhead of the per-patch spectral encoder for very high channel counts (e.g., 200+ channel EnMAP) is only partially explored; downsampled channels (64) were used during pre-training, which slightly complicates claims about scaling to arbitrary channel counts.

Comparison in Tab. 1 is somewhat self-serving (designed around the four properties CARL satisfies); a more neutral capability taxonomy or quantitative comparison per property would strengthen the positioning.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important problem: camera heterogeneity in spectral imaging that prevents cross-silo pre-training and knowledge transfer.

The proposed architecture is clearly described, with a sensible disentanglement of spectral (wavelength-aware, cross-attention to K learnable spectral representations) and spatial encoding, supported by pseudocode and reasonable ablations (positional encoding scaling, aggregation, K, embedding dimension).

Evaluation breadth is a clear strength: three application domains (medical, automotive, satellite), eleven remote-sensing benchmarks including out-of-distribution sensors, both simulated (Gaussian and real-world filter) and real cross-camera variations, plus a computational complexity analysis (Tab. 11).
Comparison against a broad set of recent, relevant baselines (DOFA, SMARTIES, Copernicus-FM, SpectralGPT, HyperFree, Hyve, Spectral Adapter) with confidence intervals reported.
The analysis of feature variance (Tab. 13) and the t-SNE disentanglement analysis (Fig. 6) provide evidence beyond raw task metrics that representations are semantic rather than sensor-driven.
weaknesses: Limited novelty at the component level: the method is largely a combination of established techniques — Fourier feature positional encodings (Tancik et al.), Perceiver-style learnable latent tokens with cross-attention, I-JEPA, and VICReg. The claim of being the 'first' camera-agnostic spatio-spectral SSL framework rests on a specific conjunction of properties rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the related-work taxonomy (Tab. 1) is constructed to favor this framing.

Cross-model comparisons are confounded by pre-training data: CARL is pre-trained on ~800k images of its choosing (HySpecNet-11k, SpectralEarth, BigEarthNet), while baselines (DOFA, SMARTIES, Copernicus-FM, SpectralGPT) were pre-trained on their own corpora. Differences in pre-training data volume and composition cannot be disentangled from the architectural contribution, weakening the central claim that camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding is the source of the advantage.

Statistical support for headline claims is thin in places: on HSICity (Tab. 2), CARL-SSL's 50.1 mIoU over DOFA's 49.6 comes with substantially overlapping 95% confidence intervals; the average-rank argument in Tab. 4 masks clear losses on individual benchmarks (e.g., 84.4 vs. SMARTIES' 92.6 on m-eurosat).

One of the three validation domains (medical imaging) uses a private, non-public porcine organ dataset, which undermines the reproducibility statement and prevents independent verification of a substantial portion of the experimental evidence.

Computational cost is non-trivial: CARL requires 286 GFLOPs on Gaofen-5 versus 32 for channel-invariant baselines, and the paper acknowledges this; the claimed mitigation via channel subsampling is evaluated only in a single setting.

Some experimental design choices appear ad hoc and are justified post hoc, e.g., manually adding Cityscapes images containing 'pole' labels to the training set, or the reduced-budget ablation in Tab. 3c, which may not generalize to the full training regime.

strengths: Addresses a real and important bottleneck in spectral imaging: camera-specific data silos with heterogeneous channel dimensionality and wavelength coverage. The problem is well-motivated and the positioning (Table 1) clearly identifies a genuine gap: no prior method combines wavelength-awareness, channel-invariance, spatio-spectral encoding, and spatio-spectral SSL pre-training.

The proposed spectral encoder (wavelength positional encoding + self-attention/cross-attention with K learnable spectral tokens) is a clean, sensible design that resolves the spectral dimension per patch and remains compatible with standard ViT-based spatial encoders, making it broadly adoptable.

CARL-SSL is a coherent end-to-end camera-agnostic spatio-spectral self-supervision framework combining a spectral VICReg objective with I-JEPA-style spatial pre-training; the ablation (Tab. 3c) convincingly shows spectral SSL prevents representational collapse (+10.5 OA).

Unusually broad and convincing evaluation across three application domains (medical in-silico, automotive, satellite), with strong and appropriate baselines (camera-specific U-Net/SwinMask2Former, Spectral Adapter, Hyve, HyperFree, DOFA, Copernicus-FM, SMARTIES, SpectralGPT, Galileo, Croma) and a unified training protocol.

Demonstrates both simulated and real-world cross-camera variation, including OOD sensors (Tab. 5, Tab. 9) with a best average rank (1.6) across 11 benchmarks, and qualitative evidence of cross-modality knowledge transfer (e.g., 'pole' class transfer from Cityscapes to HSICity, Tab. 3b).
Thorough ablations (positional encoding sigma, aggregation strategy, K, embedding dimension) with the interesting finding that K=8 suffices and gains come from embedding dimension.

Good analysis beyond headline metrics: computational complexity comparison (Tab. 11) showing favorable scaling vs. SpectralGPT, channel-subsampling as camera-agnostic augmentation (-75% FLOPs at ~equal mIoU), t-SNE and variance-decomposition analysis (Tab. 13) supporting genuine disentanglement of semantics from sensor.

Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, pseudo-code for both forward pass and training step, public datasets for Secs. 4.2-4.3, per-class IoU reporting, and claimed public release of code and weights; limitations (compute cost, non-spectral heterogeneity) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is moderately incremental: the design combines known components — Fourier feature positional encodings (Tancik et al.), Perceiver-style cross-attention to learnable latents for variable-length channel compression, I-JEPA, and VICReg. The primary novelty is their combination and application to camera-agnostic spatio-spectral learning; wavelength positional encodings already appear in DOFA, SMARTIES, HyperFree, etc.

Statistical significance of headline gains is not always clear: confidence intervals in Tab. 2 overlap substantially across methods (e.g., CARL 48.6 [45.6;51.0] vs. CARL-SSL 50.1 [47.2;52.4] vs. DOFA 49.6 [46.8;51.6]), and no formal significance testing is reported.

On some in-distribution benchmarks CARL is not the best method (e.g., SMARTIES achieves 92.6 vs. CARL's 84.4 on m-eurosat), so the claim of overall superiority rests mainly on the average rank and OOD performance.
The medical experiment relies on a private porcine organ dataset, limiting reproducibility of that portion of the evaluation.

The practical 'any channel dimensionality' claim is somewhat weakened by the channel subsampling to at most 32 channels during training (and to 64 during pre-training), so behavior on very high channel counts at full resolution is not fully validated end-to-end.
Higher computational cost than purely spatial/adaptive-embedding approaches is acknowledged but only partially mitigated; the trade-off analysis is qualitative in part.
Some claims of being 'the first' would benefit from more careful hedging given the fast-moving related literature (e.g., Panopticon, Fleximo cited only in passing).
